article.headline: Factory's Droids Seek to Automate the Entire Software Development Cycle
article.lede: A Silicon Valley startup called Factory has launched autonomous software agents it calls **Droids**, positioning them as a replacement for much of the human work in a development pipeline — from writing features off a ticket to debugging incidents and reviewing pull requests. The company, backed by Sequoia, NEA, NVIDIA, and JPMorgan in a $50 million Series B, claims its agents hit the top spot on *Terminal Bench*, the benchmark used to compare AI coding tools. The post announcing the launch is promotional in register but the underlying product is substantive enough to examine on its merits.
article.body:
Factory's central claim is that software development is moving from *autocomplete* — the paradigm of tools like GitHub Copilot or Cursor, which suggest the next line — to *delegation*, where an agent is handed an entire task and returns a finished artifact. CEO Matan Grinberg, who studied string theory at Berkeley before pivoting to infrastructure software, frames this as the largest shift in development practice since the migration to the cloud. Whether or not that framing survives contact with daily engineering reality, the distinction is real: Droids are designed to open a ticket, write the code, run tests, and close the ticket without a human in the loop at each step.

The platform is deliberately agnostic in its dependencies. Factory's Droids can run against any major *large language model* (the AI systems that generate code), inside any IDE, and can be triggered from Slack, a terminal, a browser, or Linear — the project-management tool widely used by engineering teams. That flexibility is a deliberate contrast with tools that lock users into one model or one interface. It also means enterprises can route sensitive codebases through an on-premises model rather than sending proprietary source code to a third-party API.

The investor roster signals both the capital and the strategic ambitions behind the company. NVIDIA and JPMorgan are not typical early-stage bets; their presence alongside Sequoia and NEA suggests Factory is pitching itself as infrastructure, not a developer toy. Reported enterprise customers include EY, MongoDB, Zapier, Bayer, and Clari. Usage-based pricing — customers pay for what the agents actually do — is the business model, which the company says produces surprisingly strong margins given that inference costs are its primary variable expense.

The specific capabilities the launch lists are worth parsing individually. End-to-end feature development from a prompt is the flashiest claim; *incident resolution* — having an agent investigate a production outage, write a root-cause analysis, and propose a fix — is arguably more novel and more immediately valuable, since on-call work is both costly and miserable. PRD (*product requirements document*) generation from a Slack thread and automatic *Linear* ticket management are productivity multipliers rather than replacements for human judgment, and the PR-review feature exists in several competing tools already.

The competitive framing in the original post — that Factory has "destroyed" Devin, OpenAI's Codex, and Cursor — is promotional exaggeration that the research sources do not support. *Terminal Bench* rankings measure specific task completion in controlled conditions; no benchmark yet captures the full complexity of a production engineering environment. Devin, from Cognition AI, and Cursor remain active, well-funded products. The honest picture is a crowded, fast-moving market in which Factory has staked a defensible position around flexibility, enterprise deployment, and benchmark performance — not a knockout.

concepts.definition: A development paradigm in which autonomous AI agents handle complete tasks end-to-end — writing code, running tests, closing tickets — rather than merely suggesting the next line for a human to accept. It is contrasted with the copilot or autocomplete model popularized by GitHub Copilot.

A benchmark suite used to evaluate AI coding agents on real-world software engineering tasks. Tools like Claude Code and Cursor are measured against it. A top ranking indicates strong task-completion performance in controlled evaluations, though real-world results vary.

A design choice in which a software platform does not depend on any single large language model. Users can route tasks to OpenAI, Anthropic, or a locally hosted model, giving enterprises control over cost, data privacy, and vendor lock-in.

A structured post-incident report that explains why a production failure occurred and what changes will prevent recurrence. Writing RCAs is a standard — and often tedious — obligation for on-call engineers after outages.

article.fact_check: The claim that Factory has 'destroyed' Devin, OpenAI's Codex, and Cursor is not supported by the research sources. The evidence cited is a #1 ranking on Terminal Bench, a controlled benchmark — not a comprehensive head-to-head in production environments. Devin and Cursor are active, funded products. The framing is marketing hyperbole, not a verified technical conclusion.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
